Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

vignette:
Ingrid Halvorsen is a 76-year-old widowed Norwegian-American woman who has captained commercial vessels along the Pacific Northwest coast for the better part of four decades. She came to the clinic eight months after an incident that, by her own account, she had not fully spoken about to anyone until now.

It happened on a late afternoon in the port city where she keeps her residence between voyages. Ingrid had been walking back from the harbormaster's office when she witnessed a young man being stopped by two police officers in the parking lot adjacent to the pier. What began as a verbal exchange escalated with a speed she still cannot fully account for. Within moments, one officer had the man face-down on the asphalt, a knee pressed into his back, while the second struck him repeatedly with a baton across his shoulders and the back of his head. Ingrid stepped forward and identified herself, calling out that she was watching and that the force was unnecessary. The officer who had been standing turned on her instead. She was shoved hard against a chain-link fence, her wrists wrenched behind her back, her face pressed against the metal. She could feel the cold of the links against her cheek, hear the officer's voice close to her ear telling her to stop resisting - though she had not been resisting - and she remembers with absolute clarity the smell of rust and brine, the sound of the young man still crying out on the ground, and the particular quality of the late light falling flat and grey across the water behind the officer's shoulder. She was detained for approximately forty minutes before being released without charge.

In the weeks that followed, Ingrid found herself returning to that afternoon with an involuntary precision that alarmed her. Her memories of it were not fragmentary or vague - they were, as she described it, like slides projected in sequence: the officer's face, the angle of the fence, the grey water, the sound. When these images came, they did not feel like recollection. They felt immediate, as though she were still pressed against that fence, still hearing the voice at her ear. She would be standing at the helm in open water, hands steady on the wheel, and the smell of salt air would fold without warning into that parking lot, and she was there again, not here.

She began to manage this by staying on the water as much as possible, taking on additional contracts, volunteering for longer hauls. On the bridge, with a crew and a course and a radio and a log to maintain, the demands of the present were loud enough to compete. She told herself this was simply what she had always done - worked hard, kept moving. But the port itself had become something she dreaded. Docking meant the walk back along the pier, meant the harbormaster's parking lot sitting at the edge of her vision, meant the chain-link fencing that ran the length of the maintenance yard. She began arranging for her first mate to handle dockside paperwork that she had always managed herself. Over several months, her presence on land contracted to the bare minimum. Her relationship with the harbormaster's office - professional, collegial over many years - grew noticeably cooler, and she is aware that colleagues have remarked on her unavailability in ways that have begun to affect her professional standing.

In quieter moments, Ingrid goes over and over the question of why it happened to her - a woman of her age and standing, someone who had spent her life commanding respect and maintaining order. She dwells on who she was before: capable, unafraid, someone who walked into any room or any port without a second thought. She had come to believe that something essential had been taken from her that afternoon, something she could not name precisely but whose absence she felt constantly. What finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with her adult daughter, who told her plainly that she seemed like a different person. Ingrid did not argue. What she hopes for, she said carefully, is to be able to walk back along that pier without feeling like she is still there. What she fears is that she no longer knows how.
